S1|run1.question: In the ENCOMPASS paper, what does PAN stand for and what two concerns does the programming model separate?
S1|run1.answer:
PAN stands for **“probabilistic angelic nondeterminism”**: the paper says, “we introduce probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN)” [conf_nips_li2025encompass p.1], and later “call this programming model probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN)” [conf_nips_li2025encompass p.2].

The programming model separates **“inference-time algorithms (search policy)”** from **“the underlying logic of the agent (specification of the search space)”** [conf_nips_li2025encompass p.2]. The abstract also describes this as separating “the core workflow logic and the inference-time strategy” [conf_nips_li2025encompass p.1].

In this section, we introduce the PAN programming model (Section 2.1) and describe its Python im-
plementation in the ENCOMPASS framework (Section 2.2). For simplicity, we will ignore the feature
of memory sharing across different program execution paths (see Section 3.2). The documentation
for ENCOMPASS is in Appendix B and the ENCOMPASS compiler is described in Appendix C.
2.1 Probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN)
The core idea of PAN is to search over the tree of possible execution paths of a probabilistic program
— where some operations (e.g., LLM calls) have randomness — to find the path that optimizes a
user-specified objective. Given a probabilistic program with branchpoints at certain locations in the
program, we model its computation as a Markov chain over the space of possible program states. The
Markov chain consists of the following components:
• Branchpoints and the end of the program constitute a set of marked locations in the program.
In Figure 1, branchpoints are denoted by blue dots .
• A program state is a pair consisting of a marked location of the program and a memory state,
which is a mapping from variables to values.
• The code that executes from one marked location to the next defines a probabilistic transition
function that maps from a program state to the next program state. Program states at the end

ming paradigm that separates the two main concerns of probabilistic inference: specifying the

experiment with different probabilistic inference algorithms. Similarly, ENCOMPASS aims to separate

Abstract
We introduce a new approach to agent programming, the development of LLM-
based agents. Current approaches to agent programming often entangle two aspects
of agent design: the core workflow logic and the inference-time strategy (e.g., tree
search). We introduce probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN), a programming
model that disentangles these two concerns, allowing the programmer to describe
the agent workflow and independently experiment with different inference-time
strategies by simply changing a few inputs. We provide an implementation of
PAN in Python as the ENCOMPASS framework, which uses a Python decorator to
compile agent workflow programs into a search space. We present three case studies
that demonstrate how the framework lets the programmer quickly improve the
reliability of an agent and easily switch between different inference-time strategies,
all with little additional coding.

Recent work has shown the power of scaling inference-time compute for LLMs [1, 2], where popular

by specifying each node’s branching factor, i.e., the number of children to sample. For example,
depth-first search (DFS) with branching factor 3 involves sampling 3 next states from the current
state and recursing on each child.
This way of adapting graph search algorithms is currently the dominant approach in LLM-based
agents that have tree search with an unenumerable action space of LLM outputs [8, 13, 24, 25].
However, we believe it is worth exploring search strategies beyond fixing the branching factor in an
existing graph search algorithm, and Case Study 3 (Appendix A.2) explores this direction by showing
that a simple strategy — repeatedly choosing the highest-scoring program state and sampling one
next state — can work quite well.

is implemented as the @encompass.compile function decorator, which makes several new primitive

decorator compiles the function body into a search space object, which provides an interface for
implementing search algorithms (Appendices B.2 and B.3). The compiler is described in Appendix C.

S2|run1.question: How many Python functions are in the CRUXEval benchmark, and what two tasks does each function support?
S2|run1.answer:
The benchmark has **800 Python functions**. As stated, “**CRUXEval consists of 800 distinct functions**” [DBLP_conf_icml_GuRLSS024 p.3], and “**a benchmark consisting of 800 Python functions**” [DBLP_conf_icml_GuRLSS024 p.1].

Each function supports two tasks:
1. **Output prediction** — “**the goal is to predict the output of executing the function on its associated input**” [DBLP_conf_icml_GuRLSS024 p.3].
2. **Input prediction** — “**the goal is to find any input such that executing the function on that input produces the output**” [DBLP_conf_icml_GuRLSS024 p.3].

S3|run1.question: What does LINC stand for, and what role does the language model play in it?
S3|run1.answer:
LINC stands for **“Logical Inference via Neurosymbolic Computation”** [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.1]. The paper says that in LINC, **“the LLM acts as a semantic parser, translating premises and conclusions from natural language to expressions in first-order logic”** [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.1], and more specifically, **“the LLM acts as a semantic parser, translating NL statements into FOL expressions”** [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.3].

It also says that the logical inference itself is handled by an external prover: **“These expressions are then offloaded to an external theorem prover, which symbolically performs deductive inference”** [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.1].

S4|run1.question: What are the three pillars of machine programming, and what does each emphasize?
S4|run1.answer:
The three pillars are **intention, invention, and adaptation**. The paper states: “Those pillars are: (i) intention, (ii) invention, and (iii) adaptation” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1].

What each emphasizes:

- **Intention**: “advancements in the human-to-computer and computer-to-machine-learning interfaces” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1]. More specifically, it is “the ability of the machine to understand the programmer’s goals through more natural forms of interaction” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2].

- **Invention**: “the creation or refinement of algorithms or core hardware and software building blocks through machine learning (ML)” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1]. The paper also says it is “the ability of the machine to discover how to accomplish such goals; whether by devising new algorithms, or even by devising new abstractions from which such algorithms can be built” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2].

- **Adaptation**: “advances in the use of ML-based constructs to autonomously evolve software” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1]. It is also described as “the ability to autonomously evolve software, whether to make it execute efficiently on new or existing platforms, or to fix errors and address vulnerabilities” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2].

S6|run1.question: In 'Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis', how is the subset of examples chosen?
S6|run1.answer:
The subset is chosen **iteratively**. The paper says: “**Starting with an empty subset, the algorithm uses a neural network to compute the probability of all the examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset. It then adds the least probable example to the subset**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.3].

The abstract gives the same idea more briefly: “**the subset is constructed iteratively, using a neural network to predict the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset, and greedily adding the least probable example**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].

So, in short: it starts empty, predicts probabilities conditioned on the current subset, and greedily adds the example with the lowest probability.

S7|run1.question: In 'The Counterfeit Conundrum', what two properties define a counterfeit sample?
S7|run1.answer:
A counterfeit sample is defined by two properties:

1. It is “a program sampled from a code language model which is 1) good enough to be generated by the language model at a moderate temperature” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1].
2. It “pass[es] weak but nontrivial correctness checks” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1].

The paper also restates this as samples that “have a high enough log-probability to be generated at a moderate temperature” and “pass weak correctness checks” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2402-19475 p.3].

N2|run1.answer:
In the Lynx paper, the programmatic SAT solver is applied to the **RNA-folding problem**, specifically **“the RNA secondary structure prediction problem.”** The paper states: “Lynx: A Programmatic SAT Solver for the RNA-Folding Problem” and says, “We demonstrate the benefits of Lynx through a case-study from computational biology, namely, the RNA secondary structure prediction problem” [DBLP_conf_sat_GaneshOSDRS12 p.1].

N3|run1.question: What does the SPARLING method learn, and what does its main theorem state?
N3|run1.answer:
SPARLING is described as learning “spatial concept[s]” / “sparse and local latent intermediate variables, which we call motifs” [conf_iclr_gupta2025sparling p.1]. The abstract says these motifs are “an extremely sparse activation tensor” and that SPARLING is an algorithm for identifying them [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2302-01976 p.1].

Its main theorem is the “Motif Identifiability Theorem,” which states that “under certain assumptions it is possible to precisely identify these motifs exclusively by reducing end-to-end error” [conf_iclr_gupta2025sparling p.1]. The abstract also emphasizes that they “do not assume identifiability of parameters, but rather of a latent intermediate representation output by a local model” [conf_iclr_gupta2025sparling p.1].

N4|run1.question: In the LINC paper, what limits the setting the authors consider, and what effect does that limitation have?
N4|run1.answer:
The paper says the setting is limited by the **narrow scope of the logical reasoning task**: “we focus exclusively on one aspect of logical reasoning: **predicting the truth value of a conclusion given a set of natural language premises**” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9]. It also says this is “a setting where the” model has to reason over a premise set, and that the work “consider[s] a setting where the” premises are limited in the in-context examples compared with evaluation on “a much larger set of premises” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

The effect of this limitation, according to the paper, is that LINC’s strengths are shown within that restricted task, but the authors frame it as incomplete coverage of logical reasoning generally. They say their experiments show “significant performance gains in nearly every setting we consider,” and that LINC “supports generalization to settings where the model has to reason about a much larger set of premises than it is shown in the in-context learning examples” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9]. They also note that future work is needed because “more elegant handling of naturalistic language use” is a key opportunity for improvement [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.15].

C1|run1.question: How do different papers in this collection define the program synthesis problem, and where do their definitions disagree?
C1|run1.answer:
The excerpts give only a limited view of how these papers frame **program synthesis**, and they do **not** provide multiple conflicting formal definitions. What they do show is:

1. **Synthesis as constructing a program from a specification**
   - One paper says: “**Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].
   - Another says synthesis is “**a special class of regression problems where rather than minimizing the error on an example dataset, one seeks an exact fit of the examples in the form of a program**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].

2. **Synthesis as searching a candidate program space**
   - The FMSD paper adds that syntax-guided synthesis “**starts with a structural hypothesis describing the shape of possible programs, and then searches through the space of candidates until it finds a solution**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].
   - It further distinguishes “**explicit search**” from “**symbolic search**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].

3. **Synthesis as fitting examples under a DSL plus specification**
   - The ICML paper says: “**There are two key ingredients to a synthesis problem: a domain specific language (DSL for short) and a specification**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].
   - It also says “**The DSL defines a space of candidate programs**” and “**The specification is commonly expressed as a set of input-output examples**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].

### Where they disagree
Based on the excerpts alone, they do **not clearly disagree on the core idea**. Both treat synthesis as finding a program that satisfies a specification/examples.

The only visible difference is **emphasis and framing**:
- The FMSD paper emphasizes **structural hypotheses** and **search procedures** [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].

1 Introduction
Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification. One popular
style of program synthesis is syntax-guided synthesis, which starts with a structural hypothesis
describing the shape of possible programs, and then searches through the space of candidates
until it finds a solution. Recent years have seen a number of successful applications of syntax-
guided synthesis, ranging from automated grading [21], to programming by example [9], to
synthesis of cache coherence protocols [25], among many others [6,17,23].

stochastically or systematically enumerating the candidate program space—and others use
symbolic search—encoding the search space as constraints that are solved using a SAT solver.
The SyGuS competition has recently revealed that neither approach is strictly better than the
other [1].

C2|run1.question: What different strategies do these papers use to combine language models with formal verification or symbolic reasoning?
C2|run1.answer:
The excerpts mention several different ways to combine language models with symbolic reasoning or formal methods:

1. **Fine-tune an LM to propose facts, then use a symbolic reasoner**
   - “Zhang et al. (2022) finetune a language model to synthesize potential facts paired with likelihoods and then use a handwritten differentiable symbolic reasoner in order to deduce other facts” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

2. **Relax the solver and train neural models to choose rule applications**
   - “Weir and Van Durme (2022) relax the solver by instead training neural ‘entailment’ models to decide if and how a given inference rule applies at each stage” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

3. **Neurosymbolic reasoning with declarative prompting / LINC-like approaches**
   - The excerpt says “Logic-LM (Pan et al., 2023) and SATLM (Ye et al., 2023) propose neurosymbolic approaches which have much in common with LINC” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].
   - It also notes SATLM uses “an FOL representation” that the authors “believe is easier for humans to read and models to learn” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

4. **Autoformalization: translate natural language into symbolic languages**
   - “The idea of automatically translating natural language into structured symbolic representations that programs can reason about” is called “autoformalization” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].
   - The excerpt gives examples in theorem proving systems like “Mizar,” “Lean 3,” and “Isabelle,” and also temporal logic [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

5. **Tool usage: augment language models with external tools**
   - “The central idea in this line of research is to augment language models with external tools such as calculators, code interpreters and information retrieval systems” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].
   - The excerpt says these works are divided into classes, though the second class is cut off [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9].

6. **Modular reasoning for synthesis using function models**
   - The VMCAI paper describes “a mechanism of modular reasoning for synthesizing complex sketches, where we use function models to specify the behavior of constituent function components” [DBLP_conf_vmcai_SinghSXKS14 p.2].
   - It explains that “A function model consists of three components: pre-processing code... an uninterpreted function... and a post-condition” and may also include “a pre-condition” [DBLP_conf_vmcai_SinghSXKS14 p.2].

7. **Compositional verification by breaking a task into smaller proofs**
   - The excerpt says “reasoning based approaches perform compositional verification by breaking down the verification task of a system into smaller tasks that involve verification of individual components” [DBLP_conf_vmcai_SinghSXKS14 p.2].

What the excerpts do **not** provide is a full comparison of all possible hybrid strategies; they only explicitly describe the strategies above.

C3|run1.answer:
The excerpts mention several benchmarks for evaluating code-generating language models, but they do not give full descriptions for all of them. Here is what they explicitly say:

- **HumanEval**: “the initial standard for evaluating code generation was HumanEval” and it is described as a benchmark that tests “the ability to generate short code snippets from natural language specifications” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.2]. Another excerpt says it was “followed by MBPP” and is one of the benchmarks that “primarily focus on natural language to Python code generation” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

- **MBPP**: described as “for standard-library reliance” in one excerpt, and in another as a benchmark that “test[s] the ability to generate short code snippets from natural language specifications” [DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18 p.2; DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.2]. It is also listed among benchmarks that “primarily focus on natural language to Python code generation” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

- **APPS**: named as a benchmark “for competitive programming” [DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18 p.2] and also included among benchmarks that “primarily focus on natural language to Python code generation” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

- **CRUXEval**: introduced as “a new benchmark, CRUXEval (Code Reasoning, Understanding, and eXecution Evaluation) with two tasks: 1) output prediction, CRUXEval-O to measure code execution following and 2) input prediction, CRUXEval-I to measure code reasoning and understanding” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.2]. It “examines the abilities of code LMs to reason about the execution behaviour of simple Python programs” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.2].

- **HumanEval+**: listed among “Many benchmarks” proposed to compare and evaluate code models, alongside HumanEval, APPS, Code-Contests, MBPP, and L2CEval, but the excerpt does **not** explain what it measures [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

- **Code-Contests**: similarly listed among benchmarks, but the excerpt does **not** state what it measures [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

- **L2CEval**: listed among benchmarks, but no measurement description is given in the excerpt [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

- **DS-1000**: mentioned as one of the “Benchmarks like” those that “have focused on code generation in APIs,” but the excerpt cuts off before giving its specific measurement target [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

- **ARCADE**: also named in the same API-oriented list, but the excerpt does not explain its exact measure [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

- **NumpyEval**: listed in the API-oriented benchmark examples, but the excerpt does not specify what it measures [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

In short, the excerpts explicitly characterize:
- **HumanEval / MBPP / APPS** as benchmarks for **code generation** from natural language, with HumanEval and MBPP specifically said to test generation of short snippets, MBPP also tied to standard-library reliance, and APPS to competitive programming [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.2; DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18 p.2].
- **CRUXEval** as a benchmark for **code reasoning, understanding, and execution** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.2].

The other benchmark names appear in the excerpts, but their measurement goals are not described there.

C4|run1.question: Across these papers, what reasons are given for why program synthesis is computationally hard?
C4|run1.answer:
The excerpts give two main reasons program synthesis is computationally hard:

1. **The underlying problem is inherently hard or even undecidable.**  
   The Fisman et al. preface says: “Program synthesis ... asks the problem whether it is possible to derive an executable implementation from a specification of a system given as a logical formula. The exact complexity of the problem depends on the type of the logical formalism and the corresponding type of systems and is either undecidable or of very high computational complexity” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].

2. **The search space of candidate programs is very large.**  
   The same excerpt explains that to “overcome the computational hardness” researchers add “some syntactic set of constraints ... in order to limit the search space of viable solutions” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].  
   Jeon et al. similarly describe syntax-guided synthesis as starting with “a structural hypothesis describing the shape of possible programs, and then searches through the space of candidates until it finds a solution” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].

3. **Searching for programs can be prohibitively expensive in practice.**  
   Ellis et al. say: “A main impediment to our use of these general techniques is the prohibitively high cost of searching for programs” [DBLP_conf_nips_EllisRST18 p.5]. They also report that synthesis “vary from minutes to hours” and that “27% of the drawings” timed out after 1 hour [DBLP_conf_nips_EllisRST18 p.5].

So, across these excerpts, program synthesis is hard because the formal problem can be “undecidable or of very high computational complexity” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1], and because synthesis requires searching a huge candidate space, which is “prohibitively high cost” in practice [DBLP_conf_nips_EllisRST18 p.5].

C5|run1.question: How do papers in this collection use reinforcement learning in connection with programs or policies?
C5|run1.answer:
The excerpts show two related uses of reinforcement learning in connection with policies, but only one explicitly uses programs.

1. **Learning programmatic policies with reinforcement learning**
   - Inala et al. say they “**propose an algorithm for learning programmatic state machine policies that can capture repeating behaviors**” and that these policies “**have the ability to generalize to instances requiring an arbitrary number of repetitions**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20 p.1].
   - They also frame this as a reinforcement-learning setting: “**Deep reinforcement learning has successfully solved a number of challenging control tasks**,” but learned policies “**typically have difficulty generalizing to novel environments**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20 p.1].
   - Their method is to learn such a policy “**by imitating a teacher**,” using “**adaptive teaching**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20 p.1].

2. **Extracting verifiable policies from reinforcement learning**
   - Bastani et al. focus on “**verifiable reinforcement learning by training decision tree policies**” [DBLP_conf_nips_BastaniPS18 p.1].
   - They explain that the goal is to “**learn policies for which desirable properties such as safety, stability, and robustness can be efficiently verified**” [DBLP_conf_nips_BastaniPS18 p.1].
   - Their algorithm VIPER “**combines ideas from model compression and imitation learning to learn decision tree policies guided by a DNN policy (called the oracle) and its Q-function**” [DBLP_conf_nips_BastaniPS18 p.1].

So, in this collection, reinforcement learning is used to **learn policies**, and those policies are represented either as **programmatic state machines** that generalize inductively [DBLP_conf_iclr_InalaBTS20 p.1] or as **decision trees** that can be **verified** [DBLP_conf_nips_BastaniPS18 p.1]. The excerpts do not show reinforcement learning directly learning full “programs” in the general sense; they specifically mention **programmatic state machine policies** and **decision tree policies**.

C6|run1.question: What roles do partial or incomplete programs play across these papers?
C6|run1.answer:
Across these excerpts, partial or incomplete programs are central as objects that must be **represented, evaluated, or reasoned about before completion**.

- In the ICLR paper, the key problem in synthesis is “**representing the behavior of a partially written program before it can be executed**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.1]. The paper says that “**execution is not always possible for a partial program**” and asks, “**How might we represent the semantics of unfinished code?**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.2]. It also notes that “**Concrete semantics cannot be used for this selection, because expressions such as x + HOLE are incomplete and cannot be executed**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.4].

- In response, that paper proposes a way to handle incomplete programs by using “**a flexible combination of concrete execution state and learned neural representations, using the learned approximate semantics when concrete semantics are not known (in unfinished parts of the program)**” [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.1].

- In the SQL synthesis paper, the role of incompleteness is different but related: unknown pieces such as loop conditions and invariants are treated as functions to be inferred. The paper says that “**the postcondition and the loop invariants are unknown when the conditions are generated**” and that “**we simply treat invariants (and the postcondition) as functions of the program variables that are currently in scope**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1208-2013 p.7]. This means the synthesis process fills in missing specifications needed to verify and derive the final program.

- The same paper shows that synthesis can infer missing logical components such as “**outer loop invariant**,” “**inner loop invariant**,” and “**postcondition**” for a running example [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1208-2013 p.9].

So, across these papers, partial/incomplete programs are not treated as finished code; instead, they are **intermediate artifacts that must be represented, approximated, or completed** so that synthesis or verification can continue [DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.1; DBLP_conf_iclr_NyePBATS21 p.4; DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1208-2013 p.7].

C7|run1.question: What different ways do these papers evaluate whether a synthesized program is correct?
C7|run1.answer:
The excerpts mention several different correctness-evaluation approaches:

1. **Exhaustive bounded checking against a specification**  
   In the recursive ADT transformation paper, the system “relies on exhaustive bounded checking to establish whether a program candidate matches the specification” [DBLP_journals_corr_InalaQLS15 p.2]. The excerpt also notes that this “does not provide correctness guarantees beyond a bounded set of inputs” [DBLP_journals_corr_InalaQLS15 p.2].

2. **Checking against weak but nontrivial correctness tests**  
   The counterfeit-program paper defines counterfeit samples as programs that “pass weak but nontrivial correctness checks” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1]. It says these checks are used to separate subtle failures from programs that “trivially fail” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1].

3. **Correctness checking via model judgment against a natural-language specification**  
   That same paper says it evaluates models on “correctness checking,” where “the model is asked to assess whether a short piece of code correctly implements a natural language specification” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1].

4. **Using interpreters for the source and target ASTs**  
   In the recursive ADT transformation paper, correctness in a benchmark is “defined in terms of interpreters for the two ASTs” [DBLP_journals_corr_InalaQLS15 p.2].

5. **Using teacher’s solution / reference implementation equivalence**  
   The automated feedback paper says Sketch “uses constraint-based reasoning to synthesize a complete program that is equivalent to the reference implementation,” and in their setting “we use the student’s solution as the template program and teacher’s solution as the reference implementation” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.10].

What the excerpts do **not** give is a single unified evaluation framework; instead, they show different papers checking synthesized programs against specifications, tests, interpreters, or reference implementations.

C8|run1.question: Where do these papers disagree about whether language models genuinely understand the code they produce?
C8|run1.answer:
The excerpts do not show a direct disagreement about whether language models *genuinely* understand the code they produce; rather, they present a nuanced tension.

One paper emphasizes limited understanding of “counterfeit samples” and says models “have a shallow understanding of these counterfeit samples” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1]. It also concludes that “models often cannot assess their correctness, reason about their execution, and struggle to repair them” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2402-19475 p.13].

At the same time, the related survey-style excerpt notes some evidence that models do capture meaningful structure: “Jin and Rinard (2023) provide evidence that LMs can learn meaningful representations when trained on programs” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2402-19475 p.13], and “Zhang et al. (2023c) explore the behavior of transformers to simulate recursive functions” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2402-19475 p.13].

So, from these excerpts, the contrast is:
- skeptical view: models “have a shallow understanding” of code they generate [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1]
- more optimistic evidence: LMs “can learn meaningful representations” from programs [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2402-19475 p.13]

But the excerpts do not contain an explicit paper-vs-paper disagreement framed as such; they mostly differ in emphasis and in the phenomena they study.

T1|run1.question: How did the stated motivation for program synthesis change between the earliest and the most recent work in this collection?
T1|run1.answer:
The excerpts show a shift from a broad, foundational goal to a more targeted, application-oriented use.

- In the earlier work, program synthesis is framed as the general problem of automatically constructing programs from specifications: “Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2]. It is also described more generally as a search problem over candidate programs: “one popular style of program synthesis is syntax-guided synthesis, which starts with a structural hypothesis describing the shape of possible programs, and then searches through the space of candidates until it finds a solution” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].

- In the more recent work, synthesis is used as a means to an end in another domain: “our work uses program synthesis to guide reinforcement learning” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2102-11137 p.19]. The same excerpt contrasts this with prior planning work and says, “our approach learns a simple straight line program that is most likely to solve the task and then replans if needed” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2102-11137 p.19].

So, the motivation changed from synthesizing programs as an end in itself to using synthesized programs as a tool to guide reinforcement learning and solve partially observed tasks [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2102-11137 p.19; DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].

1 Introduction
Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification. One popular
style of program synthesis is syntax-guided synthesis, which starts with a structural hypothesis
describing the shape of possible programs, and then searches through the space of candidates
until it finds a solution. Recent years have seen a number of successful applications of syntax-
guided synthesis, ranging from automated grading [21], to programming by example [9], to
synthesis of cache coherence protocols [25], among many others [6,17,23].
Despite their common conceptual framework, each of these systems relies on different
synthesis procedures. One key algorithmic distinction is that some use explicit search—either
stochastically or systematically enumerating the candidate program space—and others use
symbolic search—encoding the search space as constraints that are solved using a SAT solver.
The SyGuS competition has recently revealed that neither approach is strictly better than the
other [1].
In our prior work [13], we proposed adaptive concretization, a new approach to synthesis
that combines many of the benefits of explicit and symbolic search while also parallelizing
very naturally, allowing us to leverage large-scale, multi-core machines. Adaptive concretiza-
tion is based on the observation that in synthesis via symbol

As such, we do not consider this work as part of the literature on control-flow analysis. Owing to
their different emphasis, these works uniformly have three limitations that make them unsuitable
for automatically deriving CFG-generators:
(1) While they explain how a human could define a new analysis for different languages, their
analyses are ultimately manually defined for each language. They further repeat this manual
construction for every abstraction used.
(2) They check that their result safely approximates executions, but pay no attention to the shape
of the graph.
(3) Most importantly, they manually partition program states into equivalence classes. That is, they
manually annotate the program with labels or program-points, using these as CFG nodes. This
is a hindrance to both automation and theory, as most type theories do not contain labels. A
major motivation of this work is to support our ongoing work on combining analyses with
different notions of program point (i.e.: partition program states differently), which makes not
hardcoding them especially important.

mention, due to use of abstract machines and focus on generality.

T3|run1.question: How has the role of large language models in program synthesis changed over the period covered by this collection?
T3|run1.answer:
The excerpts suggest a shift from using large language models as part of program-synthesis systems to studying whether they can reliably handle more nuanced code tasks, including self-repair and debugging.

One early framing is from the synthesis paper, which says that “the synthesis methods are much more accurate than the pure neural meta seq2seq method” and that “the search-based synthesis model maintains high performance” when generalizing beyond the training distribution [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2003-05562 p.6]. It also emphasizes the classic program-synthesis advantage that “When a correct program is found, it trivially generalizes correctly to arbitrary query inputs” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2003-05562 p.6].

Later work in the collection treats large language models more directly as code systems to be evaluated on harder behaviors. For example, *The Counterfeit Conundrum* says it studies whether code language models “grasp the nuances” and notes limits in evaluating GPT-4 due to “budget constraints” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.10]. And *Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?* is explicitly about whether self-repair helps with code generation, indicating a move from pure synthesis toward repair-based generation workflows [DBLP_conf_iclr_OlaussonIW0S24 p.10].

The collection also includes systems that use program analysis and synthesis to transform code, such as StatusQuo, whose SQL extractor “uses the QBS (Query By Synthesis) algorithm to convert specific blocks of imperative code into declarative form” [DBLP_conf_cidr_CheungAMSM13 p.2].  

So, based on these excerpts, the role of LLMs appears to have evolved from being compared against or incorporated into synthesis approaches, to being evaluated as broader code-capable models for synthesis-adjacent tasks like repair, debugging, and nuanced code understanding.

T4|run1.question: What is the most recent work in this collection on code benchmarks, and how does it differ from earlier benchmarks?
T4|run1.answer:
The most recent work in this collection on code benchmarks is **LiveCodeBench**. The excerpt identifies it as “**LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Lan…**” and says, “**we introduce LiveCodeBench, a holistic and contamination-free benchmark for evaluating code capabilities**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.2].

It differs from earlier benchmarks in two main ways:

1. **It is continuously updated / live.**  
   The excerpt says, “**Live updates to prevent contamination**” and explains that “**LiveCodeBench comprises problems marked with release dates, allowing evaluations over different time windows**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.2].  
   It also contrasts this with existing benchmarks that “**may be subject to potential contamination or overfitting, as benchmark samples are present in the training datasets**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.2].

2. **It is broader than natural language-to-code only benchmarks.**  
   The paper says that “**current benchmarks like HumanEval, MBPP, and APPS may paint a skewed or misleading picture**” because “**these benchmarks only focus on natural language-to-code tasks, thus overlooking broader code-related capabilities**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.2].

The collection also shows earlier benchmark categories: benchmarks focused on “**code generation in APIs**” such as DS-1000, ARCADE, NumpyEval, and PandasEval, and others for “**broader APIs or general software engineering tasks**” and “**competitive programming**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2403-07974 p.15].

T5|run1.question: Over time, have the papers in this collection moved toward or away from requiring formal specifications?
T5|run1.answer:
The excerpts suggest the collection has moved **toward requiring or leveraging formal specifications more**, not away from them.

Evidence:
- One paper says that although “**natural language prompts offer intuitive and flexible ways to express requirements, they often suffer from ambiguity and incompleteness**,” and proposes “**enhanced specifications with more precise and verifiable representations, such as formal specifications and test-based specifications**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.33].
- It further says, “**To mitigate underspecification issues, one solution is to develop systems that can translate user intent into formal specifications**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2503-22625 p.33].
- Another excerpt makes the same point: “**while natural language prompts offer intuitive and flexible ways to express requirements, they often suffer from ambiguity and incompleteness**,” and again proposes “**formal specifications and test-based specifications**” [DBLP_conf_icml_GuJLSESS25 p.50].
- A different paper reinforces the broader trend by noting that in verification, “**Central to FV is using SVAs to encode intended behavior as formal properties**,” though “**writing accurate assertions requires deep understanding**” and is “**time-consuming and error-prone**” [DBLP_conf_fmcad_AlurBJMRSSSTU13 p.1].

Abstract. Sketching is a new form of localized software synthesis that

CRUXEval consists of 800 distinct functions, each with an input-output pair such that executing

V1|run1.question: What does RVISmith fuzz, and what does it target?
V1|run1.answer:
RVISmith is a fuzzer for **compilers**, specifically for **RVV intrinsics**.

- It is described as “**RVISmith: Fuzzing Compilers for RVV Intrinsics**” [DBLP_journals_cacm_WangZKS16 p.2].
- The paper says, “**The experiments in this work focus on only compiler fuzzing**” and that “**RVISmith can also be used to test emulators and CPUs for RVV instructions** ... **but this topic is beyond the scope of our paper**” [DBLP_journals_cacm_WangZKS16 p.5].
- It “**randomly generates well-defined C programs that include various invocation sequences of RVV intrinsics**” [DBLP_journals_cacm_WangZKS16 p.2].
- It also says RVISmith “**supports more than 98% RVV intrinsics**” [DBLP_journals_cacm_WangZKS16 p.2].

So, in short: it fuzzes **compiler handling of RVV intrinsics**, targeting **RVV intrinsic sequences in C programs** [DBLP_journals_cacm_WangZKS16 p.2][DBLP_journals_cacm_WangZKS16 p.5].

V2|run1.question: What is MANTRA, and what does it validate?
V2|run1.answer:
MANTRA is described as “MANTRA (MANual-to-Test-tRAnslation), a framework which automatically generates compliance benchmarks from natural-language procedural documents and tool schemas” [DBLP_conf_icse_JeonQFFS16 p.2]. The paper also says it “automatically generates and validates compliance benchmarks for tool-using LLM agents from procedural manuals and tool schemas” [DBLP_conf_icse_JeonQFFS16 p.14].

What it validates is the compliance of agents’ tool-use traces. The paper says MANTRA “yields high-quality trace-level compliance checks” [DBLP_conf_icse_JeonQFFS16 p.2], “constructs trace-level compliance checks to evaluate sequences of tool calls” [DBLP_conf_icse_JeonQFFS16 p.3], and uses “SMT-based cross-validation” so it can “automatically identify and repair inconsistencies before benchmark items are accepted” [DBLP_conf_icse_JeonQFFS16 p.2]. It also says it produces “validated test cases” [DBLP_conf_icse_JeonQFFS16 p.14].

V5|run1.question: What does 'Beyond the Training Distribution' map?
V5|run1.answer:
“Beyond the Training Distribution” maps **generalization boundaries** in neural program synthesis. The title and abstract say it is about “**Mapping Generalization Boundaries in Neural Program Synthesis**” and that the authors “**precisely map the data distributions**” in a controlled environment ([DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18 p.1]). The paper also says it “**systematically derive[s] in-distribution and out-of-distribution train and test splits, where the geometric distance between any test instance and the training set is known**” ([DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18 p.1]).

More specifically, it maps:
- “**the data distribution**” and
- “**generalization boundaries**” between “**density generalization**” and “**support generalization**” ([DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18 p.1], [DBLP_journals_cacm_AlurSFS18 p.5]).

V6|run1.answer:
BLK-Assist proposes “a modular framework for artist-specific fine-tuning of diffusion models using parameter-efficient methods” [source p.1]. The paper says it is “implemented as a case study with a single professional artist’s proprietary corpus” and consists of “three components: BLK-Conceptor … BLK-Stencil … and BLK-Upscale” [source p.1].

More specifically, it proposes “a modular generative AI Studio Assistant pipeline built on publicly available diffusion models fine-tuned through parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) on a singular artist’s own curated dataset” [source p.2]. The stated goal is to support “a privacy-preserving, consent-based approach to human–AI co-creation that maintains stylistic fidelity to the source corpus” [source p.1].

V7|run1.question: What is Bench-Push benchmarking?
V7|run1.answer:
Bench-Push is benchmarking “**pushing-based navigation and manipulation tasks for mobile robots**” [DBLP_conf_icra_CamposISK19 p.1].

The excerpts say it is “**the first unified benchmark for pushing-based mobile robot navigation and manipulation tasks**” [DBLP_conf_icra_CamposISK19 p.1], and also “**the first comprehensive suite of tools for standardized training and evaluation of algorithms for pushing-based mobile robot tasks**” [DBLP_conf_icra_CamposISK19 p.2].

More specifically, it benchmarks tasks where “**the mobile robot must go beyond traditional obstacle avoidance, leveraging pushing or nudging strategies to accomplish its goals**” [DBLP_conf_icra_CamposISK19 p.1]. The listed tasks include “**navigating a maze with movable obstacles, autonomous ship navigation in ice-covered waters, box delivery, and area clearing**” [DBLP_conf_icra_CamposISK19 p.1].

U1|run1.answer:
The excerpts do **not** say anything about using **CRISPR gene editing to optimize code**.

What they do contain instead is:

- A paper on **genome interpretation and RNA splicing**: “Training a new Adjusted Motif (AM) architecture on the splicing task not only yields better splicing predictions but also improves prediction of RBP-binding sites in vivo and of splicing activity” [Gupta2024 p.1].
- A paper on **code reasoning and execution benchmarks**, discussing fine-tuning and code generation/execution, but not biology or gene editing: “it remains a curiosity whether fine-tuning on execution information can help code generation abilities” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-2401-03065 p.16].
- A paper on **program synthesis with a REPL** for string editing and code execution, again unrelated to CRISPR: “We designed and implemented a REPL” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1906-04604 p.6].
- A paper on **domain-specific compilers** and **stencil computations**, discussing compiler optimization, not gene editing: “General compiler loop transformations based on the polyhedral method can optimize some stencils” [DBLP_conf_snapl_CheungKS15 p.8].

So, based on these excerpts, there is **no support for the claim that these papers discuss CRISPR gene editing as a way to optimize code**.

Stencil computations describe an important computational pattern used in many areas of
computing, including image processing, linear algebra solvers, and scientific simulations. A
stencil computation consists of updating each point in a multidimensional grid with a function
of a subset of its neighbors. Such computations are diﬃcult to optimize using libraries,
because the optimizations depend heavily on the sequence of stencils and the particular
function being applied. General compiler loop transformations based on the polyhedral
method [16] can optimize some stencils, but do not usually obtain peak performance due
to their limited scope – they only optimize traversals in an existing loop nest, and they
cannot optimize across loop nests due to a lack of high-level knowledge about the overall
computation.

Abstract
While deep reinforcement learning has successfully solved many challenging con-
trol tasks, its real-world applicability has been limited by the inability to ensure
the safety of learned policies. We propose an approach to verifiable reinforcement
learning by training decision tree policies, which can represent complex policies
(since they are nonparametric), yet can be efficiently verified using existing tech-
niques (since they are highly structured). The challenge is that decision tree policies
are difficult to train. We propose VIPER, an algorithm that combines ideas from
model compression and imitation learning to learn decision tree policies guided by
a DNN policy (called the oracle) and its Q-function, and show that it substantially
outperforms two baselines. We use VIPER to (i) learn a provably robust decision
tree policy for a variant of Atari Pong with a symbolic state space, (ii) learn a
decision tree policy for a toy game based on Pong that provably never loses, and
(iii) learn a provably stable decision tree policy for cart-pole. In each case, the
decision tree policy achieves performance equal to that of the original DNN policy.

tative metric for measuring the conciseness of a mathematical solution and demon-
strate the improvement in the quality of generated solutions compared to other
methods. Our system demonstrates that a program synthesis system (DreamCoder)
using MathDSL can generate programs that solve linear equations with greater
accuracy and conciseness than using reinforcement learning systems. Addition-

learning systems as DSLs, MathDSL outperforms the action-space-DSLs. We

U3|run1.question: What does this collection say about randomized controlled trial design?
U3|run1.answer:
This collection does **not** discuss randomized controlled trial design in the clinical sense. What it does say is about **randomized algorithm trials** and simulation of trials in synthesis and evaluation.

Relevant passages:

- It says the algorithm uses randomized trials in parallel: “**Rather than run a single trial at a time, we perform parallel trials**” and “**Each worker performs concretization randomly at the specified degree**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.7].

- It also describes using random sampling to simulate trial outcomes: “**we run the algorithm, but instead of running Sketch itself, we randomly (with replacement) pick an appropriate benchmark/degree trial result from the database and return that from run_trial**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.16].

- The search procedure shown in the other excerpt explicitly relies on repeated trials and statistical comparison: “**Since Sketch solving has some randomness in it, a single trial is not enough to provide a good estimate of time-to-solution**” [DBLP_conf_cav_JeonQSF15 p.8].

So, from the excerpts, the design principle is: **use repeated randomized trials, possibly in parallel, and compare their outcomes statistically** [DBLP_conf_cav_JeonQSF15 p.8; DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.7]. There is **no discussion of randomized controlled trial design as a methodology for human/medical experiments**.

N1|run1.question: Which papers in this collection do not use neural networks?
N1|run1.answer:
From the excerpts, I can identify several papers that are **not about using neural networks themselves**, but the excerpts do **not** provide enough to classify the entire collection exhaustively.

Papers in the excerpts that are clearly **not neural-network papers**:

- **“ReaS: Combining Numerical Optimization with SAT Solving”** — the excerpt says, “this paper is the first that achieves both end-to-end differentiability of a program and uses a SAT solver to help perform numerical optimization” and later “we use a SAT solver” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-04408 p.12]. This is about combining optimization and SAT solving, not using neural networks.
- **“First-order theorem proving Data Set”** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-07384 p.9]. This is a dataset citation, not a neural-network paper.
- **“cleverhans v2.0.0: an adversarial machine learning library”** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-07384 p.9] / [DBLP_conf_nips_ZhangSS18 p.11]. This is a library paper, not described in the excerpt as using neural networks.
- **“From image-level to pixel-level labeling with convolutional networks”** [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-07384 p.9] / [DBLP_conf_nips_ZhangSS18 p.11]. This explicitly uses “convolutional networks,” so it is a neural-network paper, not a non-neural-network one.
- **“Why should I trust you?: Explaining the predictions of any classifier”** [DBLP_conf_nips_ZhangSS18 p.11]. The excerpt only names it as a paper on “explaining the predictions of any classifier,” which does not indicate neural networks.
- **“Anchors: High-precision model-agnostic explanations”** [DBLP_conf_nips_ZhangSS18 p.11]. The title itself says “model-agnostic,” so the excerpt does not tie it to neural networks.

What the excerpts **do contain** is mostly citation lists and related-work references about interpretability, adversarial ML, and neural-network methods. For example, they cite “Methods for interpreting and understanding deep neural networks” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1802-07384 p.9] and “Synthesizing the preferred inputs for neurons in neural networks via deep generator networks” [DBLP_conf_nips_ZhangSS18 p.11], which are explicitly neural-network related.

If you want, I can go excerpt by excerpt and separate them into:
1. clearly neural-network papers,
2. clearly non-neural-network papers, and
3. papers where the excerpt is insufficient to tell.

N5|run1.question: What about sketching?
N5|run1.answer:
The excerpts say sketching is a way to let the programmer describe the high-level structure of a solution while an automated procedure fills in missing low-level details.

- “the programmer uses partial programs to describe the desired implementation strategy, and leaves the low-level details of the implementation to an automated synthesis procedure” [DBLP_conf_aplas_Solar-Lezama09 p.1]
- “a sketch—a partial program that encodes the structure of a solution while leaving its low-level details unspecified” [DBLP_conf_aplas_Solar-Lezama09 p.1]

They also emphasize that sketching is meant to improve productivity and code quality:

- “This approach allows a programmer to write clean and portable reference code, and then obtain a high-quality implementation by simply sketching the outlines of the desired implementation” [DBLP_conf_pldi_Solar-LezamaRBE05 p.1]
- “A sketch is a partial specification of the implementation” and “it affords several benefits to programmer in terms of productivity and code robustness” [DBLP_conf_pldi_Solar-LezamaRBE05 p.1]

More specifically, the later paper says sketching separates concerns and can help performance experts optimize implementations:

- “sketching allows collaboration between a domain expert … and a performance expert” [DBLP_conf_pldi_Solar-LezamaRBE05 p.14]
- “Via separation of concerns, sketching thus allows collabo-” [DBLP_conf_pldi_Solar-LezamaRBE05 p.14] (the excerpt cuts off there)

If you want, I can also summarize what sketching means in the context of these papers’ bit-streaming/StreamBit examples.

2 ENCOMPASS, a Python framework for PAN
In this section, we introduce the PAN programming model (Section 2.1) and describe its Python im-
plementation in the ENCOMPASS framework (Section 2.2). For simplicity, we will ignore the feature
of memory sharing across different program execution paths (see Section 3.2). The documentation
for ENCOMPASS is in Appendix B and the ENCOMPASS compiler is described in Appendix C.
2.1 Probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN)
The core idea of PAN is to search over the tree of possible execution paths of a probabilistic program
— where some operations (e.g., LLM calls) have randomness — to find the path that optimizes a
user-specified objective. Given a probabilistic program with branchpoints at certain locations in the
program, we model its computation as a Markov chain over the space of possible program states. The
Markov chain consists of the following components:
• Branchpoints and the end of the program constitute a set of marked locations in the program.
In Figure 1, branchpoints are denoted by blue dots .
• A program state is a pair consisting of a marked location of the program and a memory state,
which is a mapping from variables to values.
• The code that executes from one marked location to the next defines a probabilistic transition
function that maps from a program state to the next program state. Program states at the end

Angelic nondeterminism Previous implementations of angelic nondeterminism include John
McCarthy’s amb operator in Common Lisp [35] and the list monad in Haskell [36]. The main
conceptual difference is that ENCOMPASS implements a probabilistic form of angelic nondeterminism,
which samples from a probability distribution such as an LLM instead of choosing from a given set
of choices.
Probabilistic programming Our work is also inspired by probabilistic programming, a program-
ming paradigm that separates the two main concerns of probabilistic inference: specifying the
probabilistic model and implementing the inference algorithm. (See, e.g., [37] for a review.) This
allows the programmer to efficiently specify a probabilistic model in code while independently
experiment with different probabilistic inference algorithms. Similarly, ENCOMPASS aims to separate
the two main concerns of agent programming: specifying the core agent workflow and implementing
the inference-time search strategy.

Abstract
We introduce a new approach to agent programming, the development of LLM-
based agents. Current approaches to agent programming often entangle two aspects
of agent design: the core workflow logic and the inference-time strategy (e.g., tree
search). We introduce probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN), a programming
model that disentangles these two concerns, allowing the programmer to describe
the agent workflow and independently experiment with different inference-time
strategies by simply changing a few inputs. We provide an implementation of
PAN in Python as the ENCOMPASS framework, which uses a Python decorator to
compile agent workflow programs into a search space. We present three case studies
that demonstrate how the framework lets the programmer quickly improve the
reliability of an agent and easily switch between different inference-time strategies,
all with little additional coding.

Recent work has shown the power of scaling inference-time compute for LLMs [1, 2], where popular

by specifying each node’s branching factor, i.e., the number of children to sample. For example,

state and recursing on each child.
This way of adapting graph search algorithms is currently the dominant approach in LLM-based
agents that have tree search with an unenumerable action space of LLM outputs [8, 13, 24, 25].
However, we believe it is worth exploring search strategies beyond fixing the branching factor in an
existing graph search algorithm, and Case Study 3 (Appendix A.2) explores this direction by showing

next state — can work quite well.

The ENCOMPASS framework provides an instantiation of the PAN programming model in Python. It
is implemented as the @encompass.compile function decorator, which makes several new primitive
keywords available in the body of the decorated function; the full list is given in Appendix B.1. The
decorator compiles the function body into a search space object, which provides an interface for
implementing search algorithms (Appendices B.2 and B.3). The compiler is described in Appendix C.

S1v3|run1.question: According to the ENCOMPASS paper, what does PAN stand for, and which two concerns does the programming model divide apart?
S1v3|run1.answer:
PAN stands for **“probabilistic angelic nondeterminism”**: “we call this programming model probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN)” [conf_nips_li2025encompass p.2], and Section 2.1 is titled “Probabilistic angelic nondeterminism (PAN)” [conf_nips_li2025encompass p.3].

The paper says PAN “uses angelic nondeterminism to separate **inference-time algorithms (search policy)** from **the underlying logic of the agent (specification of the search space)**” [conf_nips_li2025encompass p.2]. It also summarizes this as disentangling “the core workflow logic and the inference-time strategy” [conf_nips_li2025encompass p.1].

might object that output prediction can simply be done with a Python interpreter and that input prediction abilities can be

LINC stands for “**Logical Inference via Neurosymbolic Computation**” [DBLP_conf_emnlp_OlaussonGLZSTL23 p.9]. S4v1|run1.question: What are the three core pillars of machine programming, and what does each one focus on?
S4v1|run1.answer:
The three core pillars of machine programming are **intention, invention, and adaptation** [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1].

- **Intention**: “emphasizes advancements in the human-to-computer and computer-to-machine-learning interfaces” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1]. More specifically, it is “the ability of the machine to understand the programmer’s goals through more natural forms of interaction” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2], and it “focuses on the interface between the human and the machine programming system” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.8].

- **Invention**: “emphasizes the creation or refinement of algorithms or core hardware and software building blocks through machine learning (ML)” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1]. It is also described as “the ability of the machine to discover how to accomplish such goals; whether by devising new algorithms, or even by devising new abstractions from which such algorithms can be built” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2], and it “emphasizes machine systems that create and refine algorithms or the core hardware and software building blocks from which systems are built” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.8].

- **Adaptation**: “emphasizes advances in the use of ML-based constructs to autonomously evolve software” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.1]. It is also “the ability to autonomously evolve software, whether to make it execute efficiently on new or existing platforms, or to fix errors and address vulnerabilities” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2], and it “focuses on ML-based tools that help software adapt to changing conditions” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.8].

S4v3|run1.answer:
Yes. The three pillars are **intention, invention, and adaptation**.

- **Intention**: “focuses on the interface between the human and the machine programming system” and on “techniques to discover what a program needs to do from input that is natural to express by the human” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.8]. The paper also says intention is “the ability of the machine to understand the programmer’s goals through more natural forms of interaction” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2].

- **Invention**: “emphasizes machine systems that create and refine algorithms or the core hardware and software building blocks from which systems are built” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.8]. The paper also describes it as “the ability of the machine to discover how to accomplish such goals; whether by devising new algorithms, or even by devising new abstractions from which such algorithms can be built” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2].

- **Adaptation**: “focuses on ML-based tools that help software adapt to changing conditions; whether they are bugs or vulnerabilities found in an application or new hardware systems” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.8]. The paper also says adaptation is “the ability to autonomously evolve software, whether to make it execute efficiently on new or existing platforms, or to fix errors and address vulnerabilities” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.2].

S6v1|run1.question: In the paper "Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis," what method is used to choose the subset of examples?
S6v1|run1.answer:
The paper says the subset is chosen **iteratively** using a **neural network** to estimate the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen ones, and then **greedily adding the least probable example**.

Direct support:
- “the subset is constructed iteratively, using a neural network to predict the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset, and greedily adding the least probable example” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1]
- “Starting with an empty subset, the algorithm uses a neural network to compute the probability of all the examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset. It then adds the least probable example to the subset” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.3]

So, the method is an **iterative greedy selection guided by a neural network**.

S6v2|run1.question: How does "Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis" determine which examples belong in the selected subset?
S6v2|run1.answer:
The paper says the subset is built **iteratively** by repeatedly adding the **least probable example** under a neural-network model conditioned on the examples already selected.

From the abstract: “the subset is constructed iteratively, using a neural network to predict the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset, and greedily adding the least probable example” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].

Algorithm 3 is more explicit: it says, “Require: trained committee model … approximating \(Pr(y \mid nb_{x,k}(D′), x)\)” and then “# Find the least likely input-output example” followed by  
“\((x, y) \leftarrow argmin_{(x_j, y_j)} nn(nb_{x_j,k}(D′), x_j)(y_j)\)” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.6].

So, in short, the selected subset contains examples chosen greedily as the ones the model judges **least likely given the current subset** [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1; DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.6].

S6v3|run1.question: What procedure is described in "Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis" for picking the subset of examples?
S6v3|run1.answer:
The paper describes an **iterative greedy selection** procedure for picking a representative subset of examples.

- It says, “**The subset is constructed iteratively, using a neural network to predict the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset, and greedily adding the least probable example**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].
- More explicitly, “**Starting with an empty subset, the algorithm uses a neural network to compute the probability of all the examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset. It then adds the least probable example to the subset**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.3].
- The pseudocode also states: “**Find the least likely input-output example**” and then “**D′←D′∪{(x, y)}**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.6].

So, the procedure is: **start with an empty subset, repeatedly use a neural network to estimate which remaining example is least likely given the current subset, add that example, and continue until the stopping criterion is met** [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.6].

S7v1|run1.question: In “The Counterfeit Conundrum,” which two properties are used to characterize a counterfeit sample?
S7v1|run1.answer:
The excerpts define counterfeit samples using two properties:

1. They are “programs sampled from a language model that 1) have a high enough log-probability to be generated at a moderate temperature” and 2) “pass weak correctness checks” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1].  
2. In the ODEX setting, a program is considered counterfeit if “it can be parsed successfully by ast.parse and have a length of under 500 characters” [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.13].

So, the general characterization is: **high-probability generations at moderate temperature that pass weak correctness checks** [DBLP_conf_acl_GuLJOLSS24 p.1].

C1v1|run1.question: How do the papers in this collection each characterize the program synthesis problem, and in what respects do those characterizations differ?
C1v1|run1.answer:
The excerpts characterize program synthesis in a few related but not identical ways:

1. **As constructing a program that meets a specification**
   - One paper states: “**Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].
   - It also says syntax-guided synthesis “**starts with a structural hypothesis describing the shape of possible programs, and then searches through the space of candidates until it finds a solution**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].

2. **As generating minimal fixes to match a reference behavior**
   - The feedback-generation paper says it “**leverages program synthesis technology to automatically determine minimal fixes to the student’s solution that will make it match the behavior of a reference solution written by the instructor**” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.1].
   - So here synthesis is framed as *repairing* an incorrect program so that it behaves like a known correct one.

3. **As a search problem over program space, using explicit or symbolic methods**
   - The synthesis paper explains that systems “**rely on different synthesis procedures**,” with “**explicit search—either stochastically or systematically enumerating the candidate program space—and others use symbolic search—encoding the search space as constraints that are solved using a SAT solver**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].
   - This characterizes synthesis operationally as search through a space of candidate programs.

4. **As a computational problem that may need new scalable regimes**
   - The NIPS excerpt says, “**the focus of this paper is to define the computational problem and showing why solving it is valuable**” [DBLP_conf_nips_PuEK0S20 p.1].
   - It suggests one scaling strategy is “**a compositional synthesis regime where the system communicates with the user to specify a component at a time**” and another is to “**amortize each component of the RSA model, L0, S1, L1, with neural networks**” [DBLP_conf_nips_PuEK0S20 p.1].

5. **As an underdetermined problem in program repair**
   - The machine-programming paper says “**program repair is an underdetermined problem**,” so a repair system must choose “**among all the possible patches that eliminate the symptoms of the bug**” the one that “**actually eliminates the bug without introducing other undesired behaviors**” [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.6].
   - This is not a direct definition of synthesis, but it frames the related repair task as one with many possible solutions that need further selection criteria.

### How they differ
- **Specification vs. behavior matching:** One paper frames synthesis abstractly as satisfying a specification [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2], while another frames it concretely as matching a reference program’s behavior via “minimal fixes” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.1].
- **General synthesis vs. repair:** The feedback paper is specifically about using synthesis for *automatic feedback* and minimal correction [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1204-1751 p.1], whereas the other synthesis paper is about the broader synthesis methodology and search procedures [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].
- **Algorithmic perspective:** The synthesis paper emphasizes *how* synthesis is performed—explicit search vs. symbolic search [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2]—while the NIPS excerpt emphasizes *why the problem matters* and how one might scale it [DBLP_conf_nips_PuEK0S20 p.1].
- **Underdetermined repair perspective:** The machine-programming paper highlights that in repair there are many valid patches, so the challenge is selecting the right one [DBLP_conf_mapl_GottschlichSTCR18 p.6]. That is a more repair-oriented characterization than the specification-driven one [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].

1 Introduction
Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification. One popular
style of program synthesis is syntax-guided synthesis, which starts with a structural hypothesis
describing the shape of possible programs, and then searches through the space of candidates
until it finds a solution. Recent years have seen a number of successful applications of syntax-
guided synthesis, ranging from automated grading [21], to programming by example [9], to
synthesis of cache coherence protocols [25], among many others [6,17,23].
Despite their common conceptual framework, each of these systems relies on different
synthesis procedures. One key algorithmic distinction is that some use explicit search—either
stochastically or systematically enumerating the candidate program space—and others use
symbolic search—encoding the search space as constraints that are solved using a SAT solver.
The SyGuS competition has recently revealed that neither approach is strictly better than the
other [1].

C1v2|run1.question: In this set of papers, how is the program synthesis problem defined across them, and where do their definitions conflict?
C1v2|run1.answer:
Across the excerpts, the papers define program synthesis in a very similar broad way, but they emphasize different aspects of the problem.

### Shared definition
Two excerpts explicitly define synthesis as constructing a program that matches a specification:

- “**Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2]
- “**Program synthesis (or synthesis for short) is a special class of regression problems where rather than minimizing the error on an example dataset, one seeks an exact fit of the examples in the form of a program**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1]

So, in these papers, synthesis is about producing a program that satisfies examples/specifications exactly.

### How the specification is described
The papers differ in what they treat as the specification:

- In Jeon et al., synthesis is framed generally as satisfying “**a given specification**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].
- In Pu et al., the specification is “**commonly expressed as a set of input-output examples**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].
- Pu et al. also note that synthesis has “**two key ingredients: a domain specific language (DSL for short) and a specification**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].

### Where the definitions conflict
From the provided excerpts, there is **no direct conflict** in the core definition. The papers are compatible at a high level: both treat synthesis as finding a program that satisfies constraints/examples/specification.

What differs is the **framing and scope**:

- Jeon et al. focus on “**syntax-guided synthesis**” and discuss it as a family of approaches combining “**explicit search**” and “**symbolic search**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].
- Fisman et al. describe syntax-guided synthesis as “**this area of research**” and mention works spanning “**different directions from the spectrum of research evolving around syntax-guided synthesis**” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1].
- Pu et al. frame synthesis as a “**special class of regression problems**” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1], which is a more machine-learning-oriented characterization than the other excerpts.

### Bottom line
The excerpts do **not** show a genuine contradiction in what synthesis is. They all agree it is about constructing a program that meets a specification, but they differ in emphasis:

- **general specification satisfaction** [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2]
- **exact fit to input-output examples** [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1]
- **syntax-guided synthesis as a broader research area** [DBLP_journals_fmsd_FismanSS21 p.1]

If you want, I can also compare how these papers differ in their treatment of **search strategy** (explicit vs symbolic vs adaptive concretization vs solver-internal synthesis).

C1v3|run1.question: What definitions of the program synthesis problem are given by the papers in this collection, and at which points do those definitions not match each other?
C1v3|run1.answer:
The excerpts give several related but not identical definitions of program synthesis.

### Definitions given

1. **“Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification.”**  
   This is stated in the SyGuS paper: “Program synthesis aims to construct a program satisfying a given specification” [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].

2. **“one seeks a solution, in the form of a source-code program, mapping the inputs to their corresponding outputs exactly.”**  
   The ICML paper defines it as: “Program synthesis is a class of regression problems where one seeks a solution, in the form of a source-code program, mapping the inputs to their corresponding outputs exactly” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1]. The arXiv version repeats the same wording [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.1].

3. **“rather than minimizing the error on an example dataset, one seeks an exact fit of the examples in the form of a program.”**  
   The same ICML excerpt also says: “Program synthesis (or synthesis for short) is a special class of regression problems where rather than minimizing the error on an example dataset, one seeks an exact fit of the examples in the form of a program” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1].

4. **“synthesis of a program from examples” / example-based specification.**  
   The ICML paper adds that “The specification is commonly expressed as a set of input-output examples which the candidate program needs to fit exact” [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1]. This is not a full definition of synthesis, but it narrows the kind of specification they are talking about.

### Where they do not match

The excerpts differ mainly in **what counts as the specification / target condition**:

- The SyGuS paper uses the broader formulation: **“satisfying a given specification”** [DBLP_journals_fmsd_JeonQSF17 p.2].
- The ICML/arXiv paper is narrower and example-centered: **“mapping the inputs to their corresponding outputs exactly”** and **“an exact fit of the examples”** [DBLP_conf_icml_PuMSK18 p.1; DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1711-03243 p.1].

So the mismatch is that one paper describes synthesis in terms of an **arbitrary specification**, while the other frames it specifically as **exactly fitting input-output examples**.

### What the excerpts do not show

The provided excerpts do **not** show a direct contradiction about the overall goal of synthesis: all of them present it as finding a program that meets some target condition. They just emphasize different formulations of that target condition.

Abstract
Program synthesis is a class of regression prob-
lems where one seeks a solution, in the form of
a source-code program, mapping the inputs to
their corresponding outputs exactly. Due to its
precise and combinatorial nature, program syn-
thesis is commonly formulated as a constraint sat-
isfaction problem, where input-output examples
are encoded as constraints and solved with a con-
straint solver. A key challenge of this formulation
is scalability: while constraint solvers work well
with a few well-chosen examples, a large set of ex-
amples can incur significant overhead in both time
and memory. We describe a method to discover
a subset of examples that is both small and rep-
resentative: the subset is constructed iteratively,
using a neural network to predict the probability
of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen
examples in the subset, and greedily adding the
least probable example. We empirically evaluate
the representativeness of the subsets constructed
by our method, and demonstrate such subsets can
significantly improve synthesis time and stability.
